advisories.summary: isomorphic-git: Circular symbolic references cause non-terminating resolution (DoS)
advisories.description:
### Summary
A malicious server can advertise circular `symref=` capabilities (e.g. `a → b` and `b → a`). isomorphic-git writes them to disk as loose symrefs, and `GitRefManager.resolve()` follows them with no depth limit and no cycle detection, so any later operation that resolves one of them (`log`, `status`, `checkout`, `branch`, …) **loops forever** — a persistent denial of service from a single clone.

### Details
`src/managers/GitRefManager.js` — `resolve()` only enforces a depth limit when a `depth` argument is passed (`depth = undefined` by default), and has no visited-set:

```js
static async resolve({ fs, gitdir, ref, depth = undefined }) {
  if (depth !== undefined) { depth--; if (depth === -1) return ref }
  …
}
```

`updateRemoteRefs` persists all server-supplied symrefs unconditionally. After clone the client has `refs/remotes/origin/a → ref: refs/remotes/origin/b` and `b → a` on disk; resolving either never terminates. Because the bad refs live on disk, the repo is effectively bricked for the application.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git caps symref resolution at `SYMREF_MAXDEPTH = 5` (refs.c): `git rev-parse a` returns immediately with `warning: ignoring dangling symref` — no recursion, no hang.

### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av5-circular-symref` — open in a Codespace; clone writes the circular symrefs, then `git.log` on one never returns (the runner stops it after a 20s hang):

```
[AV-5] refs/remotes/origin/a contains: ref: refs/remotes/origin/b
[AV-5] refs/remotes/origin/b contains: ref: refs/remotes/origin/a
[run] *** DoS CONFIRMED: resolving a circular symref never terminates ***
```

### Impact
A persistent denial of service via non-terminating symbolic-ref resolution (CWE-674 / CWE-835). After a single clone from a malicious (or MitM'd) server the circular refs are written to disk, so every later operation that resolves them (`log`, `status`, `checkout`, `branch`, …) hangs forever — the repository becomes effectively unusable for the application.

Impacted: any application that clones from untrusted/compromised remotes with isomorphic-git.

### Suggested fix
Add visited-set cycle detection (and/or a default maximum depth, as git does) in `GitRefManager.resolve()`; optionally validate server-supplied symref targets before persisting.

advisories.summary: SIPSorcery vulnerable to Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in SCTP SACK chunk parsing
advisories.description:
## Summary
`SctpSackChunk.ParseChunk` reads the `numGapAckBlocks` and `numDuplicateTSNs` fields (each up to 65535) directly from an attacker-controlled SCTP SACK chunk and loops that many times reading 4 bytes per iteration, with no validation of the counts against the chunk length or the receive buffer. A single crafted SACK chunk from a negotiated WebRTC peer forces reads past the end of the 262144-byte receive buffer, raising `IndexOutOfRangeException`, which is not caught by the recoverable handler and terminates the dedicated SCTP receive thread — permanently killing the SCTP association and all data channels.

## Root Cause
`src/SIPSorcery/net/SCTP/Chunks/SctpSackChunk.cs`:
- `ushort numGapAckBlocks = NetConvert.ParseUInt16(buffer, startPosn + 8);` (:141)
- `ushort numDuplicateTSNs = NetConvert.ParseUInt16(buffer, startPosn + 10);` (:142)
- gap-ack loop (:146) and duplicate-TSN loop (:154) index the buffer via `NetConvert.ParseUInt16/32` (`buffer[posn]`, no bounds check — `sys/Net/NetConvert.cs:30,41`).
`SctpPacket.ParseChunks` (SctpPacket.cs:195-203) only validates `chunkLength >= 4` and `posn+chunkLength <= length`; the counts inside the value are never checked. `RTCSctpTransport.DoReceive` calls `SctpPacket.Parse(recvBuffer, 0, bytesRead)` on a reused `recvBuffer = new byte[262144]`.

## Impact
`IndexOutOfRangeException` is a `SystemException`, not `ApplicationException`, so the recoverable `catch (ApplicationException) { … continue; }` at RTCSctpTransport.cs:345 is skipped and control falls to the generic `catch (Exception) { … break; }` at :356. The `break` exits the receive loop, `DoReceive` returns, and the dedicated `_receiveThread = new Thread(DoReceive)` (:173, started once) exits with no restart → the SCTP association and every data channel are permanently dead (denial of service).

## Proof of Concept
A negotiated WebRTC peer (post-DTLS) sends a checksum-valid SCTP packet: 12-byte common header + a SACK chunk (type 3) with `chunkLength=16`, `numGapAckBlocks=0xFFFF`, `numDuplicateTSNs=0xFFFF`. CRC32C is attacker-computable. The gap-ack loop reaches `buffer[262144]` on a 262144-byte array (valid indices 0..262143) → `IndexOutOfRangeException`.

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: post-DTLS negotiated peer sends a checksum-valid SCTP packet with a SACK chunk (`chunkLength=16`, `numGapAckBlocks=0xFFFF`). Guard: `VerifyChecksum` (CRC32C). Bypass: CRC32C is computable by the sender.
2. Processing: `DoReceive` (RTCSctpTransport.cs:286) reads into reused `recvBuffer` (262144 bytes, :280) → `SctpPacket.Parse(recvBuffer, 0, bytesRead)` (:302) → `ParseChunks` → SACK dispatch (`SctpChunk.Parse` :340-341) → `SctpSackChunk.ParseChunk`. Guard: `ParseChunks` checks only `chunkLength>=4` and `posn+chunkLength<=length` (SctpPacket.cs:195-203). Bypass: `chunkLength=16` is well-formed; the counts are never validated.
3. Sink: gap-ack loop (SctpSackChunk.cs:146) calls `NetConvert.ParseUInt16(buffer, reportPosn)` with `reportPosn` starting at `startPosn(16)+FIXED_PARAMETERS(12)=28`, climbing `+4` each iteration. Guard: none on the count. Bypass: `NetConvert.ParseUInt16` (NetConvert.cs:30) indexes `buffer[posn]` unchecked.
4. Impact: at iteration 65529, `reportPosn = 28 + 65529*4 = 262144` → `buffer[262144]` → `IndexOutOfRangeException` → generic `catch` at RTCSctpTransport.cs:356 → `break` → receive thread exits, no restart → association permanently dead.

## Bypass Evidence
- Unchecked counts at SctpSackChunk.cs:141-142; loops at :146,:154.
- `NetConvert.ParseUInt16` unchecked indexing (NetConvert.cs:30).
- `ParseChunks` validates only `chunkLength` (SctpPacket.cs:195-203).
- OOB math: `28 + 65535*4 = 262168 > 262144`; buffer is 262144 (`DEFAULT_ADVERTISED_RECEIVE_WINDOW`, SctpAssociation.cs:62). `numGapAckBlocks` alone suffices — the dup-TSN loop is not needed.
- `DoReceive` catch split: recoverable `catch(ApplicationException)` at :345 (`continue`) vs generic `catch(Exception)` at :356 (`break`); `_receiveThread` started once at :176.

## Affected Versions
`nuget:SIPSorcery <= 10.0.13` (verified present on release tag v10.0.13 and HEAD da944543).

## Dedup
NOT a duplicate of GHSA-qmvg-569h-hqrh — that fix (`fe5a1fa`) touched only `SctpPacket.cs` (the chunk-cursor zero-length infinite loop, CWE-835). This is a distinct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) in `SctpSackChunk` count loops, untouched by that fix.

## Suggested Fix
Validate `startPosn + FIXED_PARAMETERS_LENGTH + numGapAckBlocks*4 + numDuplicateTSNs*4 <= posn + chunkLen` before the loops, and/or make `NetConvert.Parse*` bounds-checked, and/or treat `IndexOutOfRangeException`/`ArgumentException` as recoverable in `DoReceive`.

---
Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

advisories.summary: isomorphic-git: Arbitrary file write outside of working tree via directory symlink during checkout (potential RCE)
advisories.description:
### Summary
`git.checkout` writes working-tree files through a directory **symlink** without checking the leading path, so a malicious repository can write **outside the intended working directory**. The defect is in isomorphic-git's checkout logic itself and is therefore **independent of the `fs` provider**. The *impact* depends on the configured filesystem; worst case is arbitrary file write on the host, e.g. injecting an attacker key into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` → remote login / code execution.

### Details
A single git tree can't hold a name as both a symlink and a directory, so the attack uses two states:

```
Commit N:    config            (mode 120000, symlink → ../.ssh)
Commit N+1:  config/           (mode 040000, tree)
               authorized_keys (mode 100644, attacker public key)
```

Checking out commit N writes `config` as a directory symlink. Checking out commit N+1 sees `config/authorized_keys` as a new path: isomorphic-git `mkdir`s the parent (`config`, already a symlink → `EEXIST`, ignored) then `writeFile`s the file, which the OS resolves through the symlink to outside the working directory. A *file*-level symlink swap is caught (the `120000`→`100644` mode change triggers an `rm`), but the **directory**-level variant is not — the payload is always a new child path, a plain `create`, so the parent symlink is never removed.

The symlink target is attacker-chosen. Besides `~/.ssh`, pointing it at the repo's own control directory — `hooks → .git/hooks` then `hooks/pre-commit`, or `x → .git` then overwriting `.git/config` (`core.hooksPath` / alias / `core.fsmonitor`) — yields RCE on the next native `git` command **without** depending on `~/.ssh` existing, since `.git/` is always present in a fresh clone.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git refuses to do this: `has_symlink_leading_path()` (symlinks.c) checks each leading path component during checkout and will not follow a symlink — the hardening behind CVE-2021-21300 and CVE-2024-32002. isomorphic-git has no equivalent check.

### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av1-symlink-hook-rce` — open in a Codespace; it builds the malicious repo, serves it locally, and runs a victim. Output on Linux:

```
[AV-1] Directory symlink on disk: …/config → ../.ssh  (→ /home/node/.ssh)
[AV-1] *** SSH KEY INJECTION CONFIRMED ***
```

**Trigger:** minimal realistic path is `clone` (commit N) + a later `pull` (commit N+1) — ordinary sync of an already-trusted repo. It also collapses to a single `clone` when the consuming app reads or writes into the cloned tree, or when a symlink already exists on disk.


### Impact

isomorphic-git is filesystem-agnostic, so exploitability and blast radius depend on the active `fs` provider — specifically whether it creates a symlink and follows it on a later write:

- **Node `fs` on Linux/macOS** (servers, CI, CLIs, Electron/desktop tooling — the common server-side use): real OS symlinks → the write lands anywhere the process can reach → **arbitrary file write on the host → RCE** (the PoC above). Highest impact.
- **Node `fs` on Windows:** `fs.symlink` typically requires privilege and throws `EPERM`, so the symlink-plant step usually fails — not exploitable by default. (A property of the OS/provider, not of isomorphic-git.)
- **In-memory / browser providers** (memfs, ZenFS, lightning-fs, custom `fs`): there is no host filesystem to escape to, so the worst case is writing **outside the intended clone directory but within that virtual filesystem** — i.e. corrupting other repos/app data the same provider holds. Bounded by the sandbox, and only if the provider implements symlink creation + following.

The CVSS above reflects the worst-case (Node `fs` on a POSIX host). Browser/in-memory-only deployments are lower severity (sandboxed integrity impact).

### Suggested fix
Before each working-tree write, `lstat` every leading path component and refuse to traverse a
symlink (mirrors git's `has_symlink_leading_path()`); optionally honor `core.symlinks=false`.

Improper Link Resolution Before File Access

advisories.summary: fastapi-code-generator: Import-time RCE via route path -> unescaped @app.get('...') decorator
advisories.description:
### Summary

fastapi-code-generator (koxudaxi) emits the OpenAPI path into the generated main.py route decorator as a single-quoted string literal (`@app.get('/u/<path>/x')`) without escaping the `'`. A `'` in the path closes the decorator string and, via concatenation, injects a live expression that the decorator argument evaluates when main.py is imported (the ASGI server imports it at startup) -- code execution, no request needed. The path is a pure data field. Verified on fastapi-code-generator 0.8.0 / Python 3 / FastAPI.

### Details

```python
@app.get('/u/'+(__import__("os").system('…') or "")+'/x', response_model=None)
def get_thing() -> None:
 pass
```

The generator post-processes output with black/isort, so a syntax-breaking payload aborts generation (DoS); a valid-Python concat (`'+expr+'`, kept valid with `(… or "")`) is written and runs at import. info.description (`description='…'`), tags, and parameter defaults are `'`-escaped; the path in @app.get('…') is the unescaped sink. Models come from datamodel-code-generator (repr-escaped, no RCE).

Not a duplicate: distinct product from OpenAPI Generator's python-fastapi backend (different codebase/template/decorator); and distinct from the operation-summary docstring sink in the same product.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates the app and merely imports main.py; the injected expression runs at decorator evaluation and writes a marker. Verified on 0.8.0.

### Impact

Code execution at import/startup in any application/CI that generates a FastAPI app with fastapi-code-generator from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced spec and imports/serves it. Estimated Critical, e.g. `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`.

### Suggested fix

Escape the path for the Python string literal (escape ', \, newlines via repr) before emitting @app.get('…'), and validate path characters.

[maintainer-report.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534357/maintainer-report.txt)
[make_spec.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534358/make_spec.py)
[reproduce.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534359/reproduce.sh)

cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

advisories.summary: fastapi-code-generator: Import-time RCE via response status-code key -> unescaped @app.get(..., responses={...}) dict
advisories.description:
### Summary

fastapi-code-generator (koxudaxi) emits an operation's extra responses into the route decorator's responses={...} dict, using each response's status-code key as a single-quoted string literal without escaping the '. A ' in a status-code key closes the dict-key string and, via concatenation, injects a live expression that the decorator argument evaluates when main.py is imported (the ASGI server imports it at startup) -- code execution, no request. The status-code key is a pure data field. Verified on
fastapi-code-generator 0.8.0 / Python 3 / FastAPI.

### Details

```python
@app.get(
 '/u', response_model=None,
 responses={
 '404' + (__import__("os").system('…') or "") + 'x': {'model': Thing}
 },
)
def get_thing() -> None:
 pass
```

The responses={...} dict is emitted only when the operation has a second (non-primary) response, so the malicious key is any additional response status. The generator post-processes with black/isort, so a syntax-breaking payload aborts generation (DoS); a valid-Python concat ('+expr+', kept valid with (... or "")) is written and runs at import. The response content-type key is NOT a sink (normalized to 'model'). info.* are repr-escaped; operationId -> function_name fails closed (DoS-resistant).

Not a duplicate: same product as the path -> @app.get('…') and summary -> handler-docstring findings, but a different field (response status-code key) and position (the responses={...} decorator dict key). Distinct from OpenAPI Generator's python-fastapi. Models come from datamodel-code-generator (repr-escaped).

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates the app and merely imports main.py; the injected expression runs at decorator evaluation and writes a marker. Verified on 0.8.0.

### Impact

Code execution at import/startup in any application/CI that generates a FastAPI app with
fastapi-code-generator from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced spec (multi-response operation)
and imports/serves it. Estimated Critical, e.g. `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`.

### Suggested fix

Escape each response status-code key for the Python string literal (escape ', \, newlines via repr) before emitting the responses={...} dict, and validate that status-code keys are numeric / a known pattern. [maintainer-report.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534524/maintainer-report.txt) [make_spec.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534526/make_spec.py) [reproduce.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534527/reproduce.sh)

advisories.summary: fastapi-code-generator: Call-time RCE via operation summary -> unescaped route-handler docstring
advisories.description:
### Summary

fastapi-code-generator (koxudaxi) emits an operation's `summary` as the generated route handler's docstring, using a triple-quoted string without escaping `"""`. A `"""` in the summary closes the docstring and, via concatenation, injects a live expression that becomes an expression statement in the handler body -- which runs when the route handler is CALLED (the endpoint is hit). The summary is a pure data field. Verified on fastapi-code-generator 0.8.0 / Python 3 / FastAPI.

### Details

```python
def get_thing() -> None:
 (
 """
 x"""
 + (__import__("os").system('…') or "")
 + """y
 """
 )
 pass
```

The generator post-processes with black/isort, so a syntax-breaking payload aborts generation; a valid-Python breakout (`"""+expr+"""`, kept valid with `(… or "")`) is written and executes at call time. info.description, tags, parameter defaults are escaped; operation description is not emitted into the function body; the summary in the handler docstring is the unescaped sink. Models come from datamodel-code-generator (repr-escaped, no RCE).

Not a duplicate: distinct product from OpenAPI Generator's python-fastapi; and distinct field/sink from the route path -> @app.get('…') decorator (import-time) in the same product -- this is the operation summary in the handler docstring (call-time).

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates the app and calls the route handler; the injected expression runs and writes a marker. Verified on 0.8.0.

### Impact

Code execution on the server when the affected endpoint is invoked, in any app generated with fastapi-code-generator from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced spec.

### Suggested fix

Escape the summary for the docstring context (escape `"""`/backslashes via repr, or strip triple-quotes) before emitting it as the handler docstring; apply the same to any free-text field rendered into a docstring. [maintainer-report.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534450/maintainer-report.txt) [make_spec.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29534452/make_spec.py)

advisories.summary: Marten's LINQ provider has SQL injection via unescaped string literals
advisories.description:
Several code paths in Marten's LINQ provider and tenant-management internals interpolated a runtime, potentially attacker-influenced value into generated SQL as a single-quoted string literal without escaping or parameterization. A value containing a single quote (`'`) could break out of the literal and inject arbitrary SQL.

The primary vector is a `Dictionary<,>` indexer **key** used in a `Where` filter — `Where(x => x.Attributes[key] == v)` — a common "filter by attribute name" / EAV pattern. It is confirmed with an executed proof-of-concept and yields filter / multi-tenant authorization bypass (returning other tenants' rows) and blind data exfiltration. Where the application permits `;`-batched statements (Npgsql default), data modification is also possible.

## Affected sinks

- `Linq/Members/Dictionaries/DictionaryItemMember.cs` — dictionary indexer key (primary, confirmed PoC)
- `Linq/Members/Dictionaries/DictionaryContainsKeyFilter.cs` — `Dictionary.ContainsKey(key)` (Newtonsoft serializer only; System.Text.Json escapes the quote)
- `Linq/Parsing/SelectParser.cs` — a constant string projected through `Select(x => new { L = runtimeString })`
- `Internal/Operations/DeleteAllForTenant.cs` — tenant id reaching per-tenant projection teardown via `IEventStore.DeleteProjectionProgressAsync` (an in-code comment wrongly claimed the value was validated)
- `Schema/DatabaseScopedTenantPartitions.cs` — tenant id inlined into `FOR VALUES IN ('...')` partition DDL
- `Events/Daemon/Internals/EventLoader.cs` (defense-in-depth) — per-tenant partition-pruning literal

## Proof of concept (primary vector)

Benign: `x.Attributes["nonexistent-key"] == "v"` returns 0 rows. Attack: `x.Attributes["nonexistent' = '' or 1=1 --"] == "v"` returns all rows. Generated SQL:

```
select d.data from public.mt_doc_doc as d where d.data -> 'Attributes' ->> 'x' or 1=1 --' = :p0;
```

## Fix

Each sink now escapes embedded single quotes (`.Replace("'", "''")`, mirroring the existing `Ordering.BuildNgramRankExpression`) or binds the value as a parameter (`DeleteAllForTenant`). Where a literal is retained for partition pruning, escaping preserves plan-time pruning while closing the injection. Regression tests lock down each vector.

## Workarounds

Until upgrading: do not pass untrusted input as a dictionary indexer key / `ContainsKey` argument / `Select` constant, nor as a tenant id into projection teardown or provisioning; and disable multi-statement command batching to limit blast radius.

## Credit

Reported privately and responsibly by an external security researcher with an executed PoC. Additional sinks found during the follow-up LINQ-wide audit.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

advisories.summary: Nginx UI: Account Takeover via Missing `RequireSecureSession` on User Management Endpoint
advisories.description: ### Summary `POST /api/users/:id` allows any authenticated user to change any other user's password without `RequireSecureSession` (2FA verification). In contrast, the self password change endpoint `POST /api/user/password` correctly requires `RequireSecureSession`. This inconsistency enables any authenticated user to take over the initial admin account (user ID 1) by simply changing its password. ### Details nginx-ui enforces `RequireSecureSession` middleware on sensitive operations such as self password change (`api/user/router.go:55`), self profile update (`api/user/router.go:54`), settings modification (`api/settings/router.go:12`), and config file deletion/rename (`api/config/router.go:16-21`). However, the user management endpoint registered in `InitManageUserRouter` (`api/user/user.go:31-68`) is mounted on the `g` router group (`router/routers.go:92`) which only applies `middleware.AuthRequired()` and `middleware.Proxy()` — **no `RequireSecureSession()`**. As a result, `POST /api/users/:id` with a `password` field in the JSON body updates the target user's password with only basic JWT authentication. No 2FA or secure session verification is performed, even if the target user has 2FA enabled. The attack flow: 1. Attacker authenticates as any user (e.g., user ID 2). 2. Attacker sends `POST /api/users/1` with `{"password": "attacker-chosen"}`. 3. Admin (user ID 1) password is changed. All existing admin tokens are invalidated (`api/user/user.go:48-49`). 4. Attacker logs in as admin with the new password. 5. Admin is locked out. ### PoC [poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26971275/poc.zip) Please extract the uploaded compressed file before proceeding 1. docker compose up -d 2. python3 poc.py ### Impact - Any authenticated user can change any other user's password, including the initial admin (user ID 1). - Full account takeover of the admin account.

advisories.summary: Gogs has DOM-based XSS via Milestone Name on New Issue Page
advisories.description: ### Summary The fix for GHSA-vgjm-2cpf-4g7c (DOM-based XSS via milestone selection) was only applied to `templates/repo/issue/view_content.tmpl` but not to `templates/repo/issue/new_form.tmpl`. An attacker can store an HTML/JavaScript payload in a milestone name, and when any user opens the New Issue page and interacts with the milestone dropdown, the payload executes in their browser via Semantic UI's `preserveHTML` behavior. ### Details GHSA-vgjm-2cpf-4g7c was patched by adding `| Sanitize` (bluemonday HTML tag stripping) to milestone name rendering in `view_content.tmpl`. However, the same milestone dropdown exists in `new_form.tmpl` and was **not** patched. In `new_form.tmpl`, milestone names are rendered with Go's default auto-escaping (`{{.Name}}`), which converts `<` to `<` etc. This prevents direct HTML injection. However, when the browser renders the DOM, the text content of the element contains the **decoded** original payload (e.g., ``). Semantic UI 2.4.2's dropdown component has `preserveHTML: true` as the default setting. When a user selects a dropdown item, the internal `set.text()` method calls jQuery's `.html()` with the item's text content. This re-parses the decoded text as HTML, creating the injected element and triggering the JavaScript event handler. ### PoC [poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26508268/poc.zip) Please extract the uploaded compressed file before proceeding 1. docker compose up --build ### Impact - Stored DOM XSS: Any user with write access to a repository can create a malicious milestone. Any other user who visits the New Issue page and interacts with the milestone dropdown will have arbitrary JavaScript executed in their browser session. - Session hijacking: The attacker can steal session cookies, perform actions as the victim, or escalate privileges.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

advisories.summary: SiYuan: Path Traversal via Double URL Encoding in `/export/` Endpoint (Incomplete Fix Bypass for CVE-2026-30869)
advisories.description: ### Summary The fix for CVE-2026-30869 in SiYuan v3.5.10 only added a denylist check (`IsSensitivePath`) but did not address the root cause — a redundant `url.PathUnescape()` call in `serveExport()`. An authenticated attacker can use double URL encoding (`%252e%252e`) to traverse directories and read arbitrary workspace files including the full SQLite database (`siyuan.db`), kernel log, and all user documents. ### Details In `kernel/server/serve.go`, the `serveExport()` function (line 314-320) processes file paths as follows: ```go filePath := strings.TrimPrefix(c.Request.URL.Path, "/export/") decodedPath, err := url.PathUnescape(filePath) // second decode fullPath := filepath.Join(exportBaseDir, decodedPath) ``` Go's HTTP server already decodes percent-encoded characters once during request parsing. The additional `url.PathUnescape()` call creates a double-decode vulnerability: 1. Attacker sends: `GET /export/%252e%252e/siyuan.db` 2. Go HTTP decodes `%25` → `%`, result: `URL.Path = /export/%2e%2e/siyuan.db` 3. Go's path cleaner sees `%2e%2e` as literal characters (not `..`), no redirect occurs 4. `url.PathUnescape("%2e%2e")` decodes to `..` 5. `filepath.Join(exportBaseDir, "../siyuan.db")` resolves to `/temp/siyuan.db` The CVE-2026-30869 fix added `IsSensitivePath()` which blocks `/conf/` and OS-level paths (`/etc`, `/root`, etc.). However, it does NOT block: - `/temp/siyuan.db` — full document database - `/temp/blocktree.db` — block tree database - `/temp/siyuan.log` — kernel log - `/temp/asset_content.db` — asset content database Note: the `/appearance/` handler in the same file correctly uses `gulu.File.IsSubPath()` to validate paths (line 447), but this check is missing from the `/export/` handler. ### PoC [poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26866234/poc.zip) Please extract the uploaded compressed file before proceeding 1. docker compose up -d --build 2. sh poc.sh ### Impact - Data exfiltration: An authenticated user (including low-privilege Publish/Reader users via the Publish service) can download the entire SQLite document database containing all blocks, documents, attributes, and full-text search indexes. - Information disclosure: Kernel log (`siyuan.log`) leaks internal server paths, versions, configuration details, and error messages.

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

advisories.summary: OpenEXR: Heap information disclosure in PXR24 decompression via unchecked decompressed size (undo_pxr24_impl)
advisories.description: ### Summary The PXR24 decompression function undo_pxr24_impl in OpenEXR (internal_pxr24.c) ignores the actual decompressed size (outSize) returned by exr_uncompress_buffer() and instead reads from the scratch buffer based solely on the expected size (uncompressed_size) derived from the header metadata. Additionally, exr_uncompress_buffer() (compression.c:202) treats LIBDEFLATE_SHORT_OUTPUT (where the compressed stream decompresses to fewer bytes than expected) as a successful result rather than an error. When these two issues are combined, an attacker can craft a PXR24 EXR file containing a valid but truncated zlib stream. As a result, the decoder reads uninitialized heap memory and incorporates it into the output pixel data. ### Details This issue occurs due to the combination of two flaws. 1. compression.c:202–205 — LIBDEFLATE_SHORT_OUTPUT treated as success ``` else if (res == LIBDEFLATE_SHORT_OUTPUT) { /* TODO: is this an error? */ return EXR_ERR_SUCCESS; } ``` libdeflate_zlib_decompress_ex() returns LIBDEFLATE_SHORT_OUTPUT when the compressed stream is successfully decompressed but the resulting output size is smaller than the provided output buffer size. In this case, the actual number of decompressed bytes is written to actual_out. However, the function does not treat this condition as an error and instead returns success. 2. internal_pxr24.c:279–287 — outSize return value ignored ``` rstat = exr_uncompress_buffer( decode->context, compressed_data, comp_buf_size, scratch_data, scratch_size, &outSize); // outSize = actual bytes written if (rstat != EXR_ERR_SUCCESS) return rstat; // outSize is never referenced afterwards. // The loop below reads the entire scratch_data buffer based on // uncompressed_size (the header-derived expected size). for (int y = 0; y < decode->chunk.height; ++y) { ... } ``` After exr_uncompress_buffer() returns success, the code does not verify whether the actual decompressed size (outSize) matches the expected size (uncompressed_size). The subsequent byte-plane reconstruction loop reads from the scratch buffer up to uncompressed_size bytes. As a result, the region between outSize and uncompressed_size consists of uninitialized heap memory, which is then read by the decoder. **Affected component** - src/lib/OpenEXRCore/internal_pxr24.c — undo_pxr24_impl() (line 261–399) - src/lib/OpenEXRCore/compression.c — exr_uncompress_buffer() (line 202–205) ### PoC Please refer to the atta [poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26002361/poc.zip) ched archive file and proceed after extracting it. 1. git clone https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/openexr.git 2. mv poc openexr/ 3. cd openexr 4. docker build -f poc/Dockerfile -t pxr24-poc . 5. docker run --rm pxr24-poc ### Impact * Sensitive information from heap memory may be leaked through the decoded pixel data (information disclosure). Trigger Condition: Occurs under default settings; simply reading a malicious EXR file is sufficient to trigger the issue, without any user interaction.

advisories.summary: Parse Server crash via deeply nested query condition operators
advisories.description:
### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can crash the Parse Server process by sending a single request with deeply nested query condition operators. This terminates the server and denies service to all connected clients.

### Patches

A depth limit for query condition operator nesting has been added via the `requestComplexity.queryDepth` server option. The option is disabled by default to avoid a breaking change. To mitigate, upgrade and set the option to a value appropriate for your app.

### Workarounds

None.

advisories.summary: Directus: Authenticated Users Can Extract Concealed Fields via Aggregate Queries
advisories.description:
### Summary

Aggregate functions (`min`, `max`) applied to fields with the `conceal` special type incorrectly return raw database values instead of the masked placeholder. When combined with `groupBy`, any authenticated user with read access to the affected collection can extract concealed field values, including static API tokens and two-factor authentication secrets from `directus_users`.

### Details

Fields marked with `conceal` are protected by payload processing logic that replaces real values with a masked placeholder on read. This protection works correctly for standard item queries, but aggregate query results are structured differently, operations are nested under their function name rather than appearing as flat field keys. The masking logic does not account for this nested structure, causing it to silently skip concealed fields in aggregate responses and return their raw values to the client.

### Impact

- **Account Takeover** An authenticated attacker can harvest static API tokens for all users, including administrators, enabling immediate authentication as any account without credentials.

- **2FA Bypass** TOTP seeds stored in directus_users can similarly be extracted, allowing an attacker to bypass two-factor authentication for any account.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in Podman. An attacker can trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by supplying a...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in Podman. An attacker can trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by supplying a container image containing crafted metadata labels. Podman's auto-update mechanism improperly trusts these image labels to determine which system services to restart. If a user runs the malicious container and auto-update processes it, arbitrary system services are restarted with the user's privileges, potentially allowing an attacker to shut down the host system when Podman runs with administrative privileges.

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in the libstdc++ component of GCC. An attacker who can provide an excessively...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in the libstdc++ component of GCC. An attacker who can provide an excessively large element count to a boolean vector (std::vector<bool>) constructor can trigger an integer wrap during internal memory calculations. This issue leaves the container in an inconsistent state, leading to out-of-bounds memory access and resulting in an application crash or a Denial of Service (DoS) during subsequent operations.

advisories.summary: The web services listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.3 through 6.3.7 counts every...
advisories.description: The web services listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.3 through 6.3.7 counts every failed CardDAV, CalDAV or Autodiscover sign-in from a proxy it trusts - one on the same machine, or one named in WebServicesTrustedProxies, whose X-Forwarded-Proto it believes - against the proxy's own address, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker who can reach the proxy to have that address banned from the server's mail listeners. The listener, off by default (WebServicesHttpPort and WebServicesHttpsPort 0), signs an account in with HTTP Basic over HTTPS for CardDAV from 6.3.3 and for CalDAV and Outlook Autodiscover from 6.3.4. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, which the server trusts when it is on the same machine or named in WebServicesTrustedProxies, the listener takes the client's HTTPS from the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto header, but it does not believe X-Forwarded-For and sees the proxy's address for every client. Each failed sign-in counted towards the auto-ban against that address, so that failed sign-ins through the proxy from anybody, under any user name, reaching MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 within 30 minutes by default) wrote an IP range that refused the proxy's address at the SMTP, POP3, IMAP and ManageSieve listeners for AutoBanMinutes (60 by default), and could write it again each time it lapsed. For a proxy on the same machine that address is the loopback address, so that a webmail on that machine, local scripts that submit mail and the other local clients of the mail listeners were shut out; for a proxy at another address that also carries mail, every mail client behind it was. Such a proxy forwarding to the listener's HTTPS port, re-encrypting, was counted against in the same way, and listing it in WebServicesTrustedProxies did not spare it. The auto-ban is on by default and AutoBanNeverBan, which spares an address, is empty by default; the listener itself went on serving the proxy.

advisories.summary: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the JSON reader of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.6 and...
advisories.description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the JSON reader of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.6 and 6.3.7 allows a remote attacker to hold the server's mail delivery threads or its REST API's worker threads, making mail delivery, the REST API and the webmail unavailable. 6.3.6 fixed CVE-2026-107574, in which reading a JSON object searched the member names already read for each new name, by keeping the names in a hash set; the set uses the standard library's hash, which takes no secret, so member names chosen to fall in one bucket of it still cost time growing with the square of their number. Against the released reader, one such object of 16 MB took about 5 seconds to read in the Linux build, and one of under 6 MB about 23 seconds in the Windows build, where objects of the same sizes with other names took under a tenth of a second. A remote unauthenticated attacker reaches the reader by mailing such an object as a TLS-RPT report, up to 16 MB once decompressed, to a hosted domain's report mailbox, where an administrator has set one; it is read on a mail delivery thread (ten by default), and those threads deliver all mail, local and outbound, so a stream of such reports stops all delivery for as long as it continues. It is also reached without an account through the reply to a password-protected message, with the message's link alone, where the REST API is on (it is off by default) and a public base URL for such links is set; and by any account through the webmail's routes granted 16 MB, and by an application's API key through the send API. Each such request holds one of the REST API's four worker threads, in the process that also serves SMTP, IMAP and POP3.

advisories.summary: The sign-in of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.22-pre2 through 6.3.7 takes for an account names...
advisories.description: The sign-in of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.22-pre2 through 6.3.7 takes for an account names that are not its address but under which the database's own comparison finds it, while the per-name lockout and the compromised-account hold are kept by the name as the client gave it. This allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing an account's password beyond the lockout's threshold, and anyone who has the password of an account held for review to sign in to it. The per-name lockout (from 6.2.22-pre2; AccountLockoutThreshold in hMailServer.ini, 0, off, by default) locks a name after repeated failed sign-ins. The hold (from 6.3.4, where the compromised-account detection is set to enforce, which is not the default) refuses an account judged to have been taken over. Both are asked, before the password, of the name the client gave: trimmed, in lower case and with a domain alias or the default domain applied. The account whose password the sign-in then checks is whichever one the database finds under that name. The databases find an account under spellings that this key counts apart. MySQL and MariaDB find it under one with accented letters in place of plain ones, and MariaDB 11.8, in a database made before 6.3.4, also under one with full-width letters, with a single letter in place of a pair of plain ones, or with characters its comparison ignores in any number. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact find it under one with full-width letters or with characters their comparison ignores in any number, and SQL Server also under one with a single letter in place of a pair of plain ones, with a character of Latin-1 in place of a digit and, for an address holding letters of Latin-1 outside ASCII, under those letters in the other case, and, under an accent-insensitive collation, with accented letters. PostgreSQL finds it under one holding a letter whose lower case under the database's locale is a plain letter, and, for an address holding letters outside ASCII, under those letters in the other case; on the build for musl (from 6.3.6) the server's own lower case folds nearly all of these too. On every database, a domain alias saved with white space at the end of its name gives such a spelling too, and on every database but PostgreSQL so does an account's bare local part where the default domain was saved with spaces at its end and no other white space (neither is the default). Each such spelling has a lockout threshold of its own, so the lockout limits the guesses at an account only to its threshold times the number of the account's spellings. That is far beyond any threshold for most addresses on MySQL and MariaDB, and without limit on SQL Server, on SQL Server Compact, the database the Windows installer uses by default, and before 6.3.4 on MariaDB 11.8. A locked name is got round under another spelling. A held account is signed in to under another spelling with its password over IMAP, POP3 and SMTP AUTH, and, where they are turned on (off by default), over ManageSieve, the REST API and the webmail. IMAP LOGIN, offered as installed, carries such spellings on MySQL, MariaDB and SQL Server Compact, and, on SQL Server and PostgreSQL, for some addresses; the sign-ins that carry a name as UTF-8 carry them for the others on SQL Server, and on PostgreSQL for those holding one of the plain letters another letter lowers to or a letter outside ASCII with another case. The same lookup mapped to accounts the names given by an OAuth 2.0 token, a client certificate, a Kerberos ticket and an OpenID Connect or SAML identity provider, where those are set up (none is by default), so that a name an issuer gave to one party could sign in to another's account; OAuth 2.0 tokens were mapped so from 6.2.0, before the per-name lockout existed. A name holding a NUL character, carried from 6.3.0 on Linux and 6.3.3 on Windows, failed the statement on MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL.

advisories.summary: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7...
advisories.description: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allow a local authenticated user to run code as the administrator who installs the product, when it is installed into a new program folder in a location whose permissions let every user write, such as the root of a drive. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but its setup lets Inno Setup make a new program folder first, with the permissions the folder above hands down, and replaces them only afterwards, tens of milliseconds later (33 to 139 milliseconds in the project's test runs). In that time any local account may make files and folders in the new folder, which keep that account as their owner, among them the Bin folder that setup then copies the programs into. Setup runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, registering the service among them, before its hardening at the end of setup takes such a folder back, and those programs load a library placed in Bin in place of the system's. The default installation under Program Files, whose folders give ordinary users read and execute only, is not affected.

advisories.summary: SQL injection in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.2.18,...
advisories.description: SQL injection in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.2.18, when the server uses MySQL/MariaDB or PostgreSQL, allows a remote attacker to alter SQL statements the server runs. On those two engines parameters are not bound: SQLStatement::GenerateFromCommand wrote each value into the statement's text as a quoted literal with a separate string replacement over the whole text per parameter, so a value holding the name of a parameter substituted after it had that name replaced, inside the value, by the later value with its own quotes, which ended the literal early and placed the later value in the statement as SQL. The row the server writes for each recipient of a queued message carries the recipient's address twice, so in the default configuration an authenticated user who may send mail reaches it by sending to an address of their choosing. A remote unauthenticated sender reaches the same statement through a message the server sends to the envelope sender, such as a delivery failure notice or an automatic reply, and, when greylisting or message indexing is enabled (both are off by default), through the greylisting record's envelope addresses or through the message metadata the server stores for IMAP SORT, which carries four header fields of a received message. An altered statement runs with the privileges of the server's database account; on PostgreSQL, whose client call runs every statement in the text it is given, further statements can follow it, while on MySQL/MariaDB, where one statement is run per call, the change is confined to the statement it is in. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact, where parameters are bound, are not affected.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

advisories.summary: Unverified ownership in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allows a...
advisories.description: Unverified ownership in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allows a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's service account or as an administrator when setup installs into, or upgrades, a program folder that accounts other than the administrators could write before, such as one made beforehand at the root of a drive. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but setup refused nothing that was already in them, or in the folders that hold the event script, the add-ons and the database scripts: a program, a library, a script or a settings file that another account owns, or whose own permissions let another account change it, is kept with that owner and those permissions, which the hardening of the folders does not take away. Setup then runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, and the service, which runs as LocalSystem or as its virtual account, runs them and the event script, so that a library such an account placed in Bin is loaded in place of the system's; the account can still change the file after the installation. The default installation under Program Files is not affected.

advisories.summary: Misinterpretation of SQL statement text in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6...
advisories.description: Misinterpretation of SQL statement text in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to have a failed database write reported to the server as successful. The layer answers a failed statement as a success when it finds the marker [IGNORE-ERRORS], which is meant only for the server's own schema statements (its upgrade scripts and the database log's tables), and statements carry values from outside - an envelope address, the user name of a failed logon, a message's headers - in their text on MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL, and in the batches of the database log on every engine. Up to 6.2.18 the marker was honoured anywhere in a statement, a value included, on MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL. From 6.2.19 it was honoured only inside a comment, but the layer read a backslash inside a string literal as an escape, which SQL Server, SQL Server Compact and PostgreSQL with standard_conforming_strings on (its default) do not, so that on those engines a value holding a backslash could make the layer take part of the statement's literals for statement text and find the marker there: on PostgreSQL from 6.3.3 for every statement carrying an outside value that holds a backslash, with no setting changed for a message delivered into a local mailbox (through an internationalised (SMTPUTF8) envelope sender) and for the IP range an auto-ban writes (named after the user name of the failed logon), and on SQL Server and SQL Server Compact for the database log, when the server logs to the database (logging is off, and the log device is files, by default). A statement run outside a transaction that then failed - a constraint, a deadlock, a lock or statement timeout, a full disk, and up to 6.2.18 a lost connection - was answered as a success, and its caller went on as if the row had been written: a message delivered into a local mailbox could be counted as delivered with no row to show it and no failure notice to its sender, and a message accepted with 250 could be left with no queue row and never delivered (up to 6.2.18, and on PostgreSQL from 6.3.3 when every recipient's address carries the marker too, which needs an address that takes any local part); an auto-ban whose IP range was not written could be logged and counted as applied, with no error reported, while the address stayed unbanned; and message metadata (written only when message indexing is on), entries of the database log and rows of features an administrator turns on could be lost without an error. On MySQL/MariaDB up to 6.2.18 the caller was handed whatever identifier the client library still held for the connection - 0, or that of an insert its last successful statement made, in whatever table - under which a queued message's recipients were then written, so that another message still in the queue could be delivered to them as well. This flaw gives a value no way to change what a statement does, and no privilege is gained.

advisories.summary: The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.0 through 6.3.3, with a MySQL or MariaDB...
advisories.description: The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.0 through 6.3.3, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, can be kept from banning an address after repeated failed logons, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing account passwords from a single address without being banned. The server makes its MySQL tables in MySQL's utf8 character set, which holds no character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, sends its statements as UTF-8 over a utf8mb4 connection and leaves the database's default strict mode in place. From 6.2.0 it decodes the user name of a SASL PLAIN logon as UTF-8, so the name can hold such a character. When the failed logons counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 by default), the server clears that address's count, saves an IP range named "Auto-ban: " followed by the user name of the logon that reached the limit, and drops the connection. If such a character is in the part of the user name that the range's name keeps (the name is cut to 100 characters), the database refuses the range: no range is saved, the address is not refused, and, its count having already been cleared, it is given the next full set of attempts. An attacker can in this way spend all but the last attempt of each set on password guesses, and make the last under such a name. On Windows, POP3 AUTH PLAIN reaches it on a server as installed, and IMAP AUTHENTICATE PLAIN where IMAP SASL authentication is turned on (off by default); on Windows and on Linux (from 6.3.0), SMTP AUTH PLAIN reaches it where plain-text authentication is allowed (off by default), and ManageSieve and CardDAV where they are turned on (off by default). Each failed save is reported in the server's error log. A database whose strict mode has been turned off stores the character as a question mark and makes the first such ban, but refuses every later ban named after the same user name, or after one holding other such characters in their place, as a duplicate while the first stands, since the server cannot look up a name holding such a character there.

cwes.name: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

advisories.summary: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 through 6.3.7, with a MySQL or MariaDB database and TlsMode...
advisories.description: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 through 6.3.7, with a MySQL or MariaDB database and TlsMode=verify-full, does not hand the database client the CA file that TlsCaFile names when the file's name contains a character outside ASCII on Linux, or above U+00FF on Windows, which allows an attacker who can intercept the connection to the database server to read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database, by presenting, with MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.2 to 3.4.10 as the client, a certificate from any authority, its own included, for any name, and otherwise a certificate for the database server's name issued by any certificate authority in the system's trust store. The server converted the name for the client with the C runtime's conversion in the C locale, which gives an empty string for such a name, and then set no CA file at all, without an error, while certificate verification stayed on, so the client - MariaDB Connector/C, bundled on Windows and the distribution's on Linux - verified the certificate of a database server over the network against the system's trust store instead of the configured CA; Connector/C 3.4.2 to 3.4.10 (bundled on Windows in 6.3.4 to 6.3.6) went further and, with no CA file, took a certificate within its dates whose issuer it could not find, for any name, with neither its chain nor its name checked and no password proof, when the server offered first a sign-in method that hashes the password, which an attacker in the middle chooses (MariaDB's CONC-853, fixed in Connector/C 3.4.11), and Connector/C 3.4 accepted from a MariaDB 11.4 or later server a certificate the store did not vouch for when that server proved it held the account's password; on a connection it treats as local (127.0.0.1, ::1, a Unix socket, a named pipe, and localhost on Windows), Connector/C 3.4.1 and later checked neither the certificate's issuer nor its name, so that a local attacker able to stand in for the database server could present any certificate within its dates of its own making. The settings line of hmailserver --check-database still named the configured file, and the application log said the certificate had been checked. With MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.1 to 3.4.9 as the client - bundled on Windows in 6.3.4 to 6.3.6, and the client of Linux distributions that have not patched it - the missing CA file also met the precondition of CVE-2026-107819, so that a certificate issued for any other name by a trusted authority was enough to obtain the database password. On Linux the file was found only when the server ran on glibc under a locale whose character set holds the name's characters (a UTF-8 locale, or a legacy 8-bit one the system has, in whose bytes the file is then named); with no locale, LC_ALL=C or a locale the system lacks, and on Alpine (musl), the connection failed instead. The configuration is not the default: TlsMode defaults to prefer, which checks no certificate.

advisories.summary: The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 can be kept from banning an...
advisories.description: The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 can be kept from banning an address after repeated failed logons, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker who can connect from two or more addresses to go on guessing account passwords - over SMTP AUTH, IMAP and POP3, and over ManageSieve, CalDAV/CardDAV and the REST API where those are turned on (off by default) - without being banned. When the failed logons counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 by default), the server clears that address's count, saves an IP range that refuses the address for AutoBanMinutes (60 by default) and drops the connection. The range is named "Auto-ban: " followed by the user name of the logon that reached the limit, and no two ranges may have the same name. The server chooses the name by checking candidates as written - the name, then the name with a number, a random suffix or a GUID added - and only then cuts it to the 100 characters the database column holds, so that with a user name of 90 characters or more every candidate is the same once cut. While one range named after such a user name stands, every later ban named after a user name with the same first 90 characters therefore fails at the database: no range is saved, the address is not refused, and, its count having already been cleared, it is given the next full set of attempts. A user name of 78 to 89 characters makes later bans fail in the same way: from the second, the third or the twelfth on, depending on its length and the database, or, from 78 to 85 characters, by chance. An attacker who has once had an address banned under such a name can in this way keep guessing passwords from any other address, ending each set of attempts with a logon under a name of that kind; each failed save is reported in the server's error log (as the database error HM5032, and from 6.2.19 also as HM6099). On SQL Server a user name holding characters outside the database's code page has the same effect at any length, because the check compared names in that code page; that save is refused by the server's own check of the name, with no database error, and is reported only from 6.2.19 (HM6099). A user name holding a NUL character, which the web services listener's HTTP Basic sign-in (off by default) carries from 6.3.3 and, on the Linux builds, IMAP LOGIN, offered as installed, from 6.3.0, makes bans fail at any length: on MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL the statements that check the name and save the range end at the character, so that every ban named after such a name fails, from the first and from a single address, and, its count having already been cleared, the address is given the next full set of attempts; on SQL Server and SQL Server Compact the name is bound only as far as the character, so that while one range under the part before it stands, every later ban named after such a name fails. On SQL Server, and on MySQL and MariaDB for an account whose local part has nine characters or more, a guess at the account can itself carry a name of that kind, since those databases find an account under its address followed by spaces (and SQL Server also under one holding characters its comparison ignores), so that not even a MaxInvalidLogonAttempts of 1, which bans each failed logon under the name it gave, avoids it there.

advisories.summary: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7...
advisories.description: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allow a local authenticated user to run code as the administrator who runs setup, when the server is installed into a program folder that is already there and that accounts other than the administrators could write, such as a folder made beforehand at the root of a drive, or when such an installation is upgraded or repaired. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but for a folder that is already there it does so only at the end of setup: setup first copies the programs into Bin, which every user may still write, and runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, registering the service among them, before that hardening, so that a library another account places in Bin meanwhile is loaded in place of the system's. A handle an account opened on such a folder while it could write it keeps that access after the hardening. The default installation under Program Files, whose folders give ordinary users read and execute only, is not affected.

advisories.summary: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 on Windows hands OpenSSL the names of its...
advisories.description: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 on Windows hands OpenSSL the names of its own TLS files - the listeners' certificates, chains, private keys and Diffie-Hellman parameters, a port's client-certificate CA file (from 6.2.19), the object store's CA file (from 6.3.4) and the ACME client's keys and certificates - as Latin-1 bytes, which on code page 1252 are the code page's own for U+00A0 to U+00FF, and OpenSSL's file opening on Windows reads a name as UTF-8 first and opens the file at that reading when it is there, or creates it there when its folder is. When every byte of a configured name outside ASCII also reads as UTF-8 - for example U+00C3 U+00A9, the bytes C3 A9, which are U+00E9 in UTF-8 - the server used the file at that other name whenever one was there, which allows a local attacker who can create that file or its folder but cannot change the configured one, as any user can by default beside a file an administrator keeps under ProgramData, to have a port that logs on by client certificate (from 6.2.25) accept certificates from a certificate authority of the attacker's own and so sign in over the network as any mailbox without its password; to have the server trust such an authority for its object store and, intercepting that connection, read and modify the messages it stores; to receive the private keys the ACME client writes, the key of a certificate issued for the server's names among them; or to keep TLS ports from starting. The configuration is not the default: by default these files have names in ASCII, client certificates are off on every port, and the object store and ACME are off. The Linux builds are not affected.

advisories.summary: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.25 through 6.3.7 on Windows, with a PostgreSQL database, the...
advisories.description: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.25 through 6.3.7 on Windows, with a PostgreSQL database, the connection's sslmode require, verify-ca or verify-full, and a root certificate file named by PostgreSQLSslRootCert (from 6.2.25) or, with TlsMode=verify-full and neither PostgreSQL key set, by TlsCaFile (from 6.3.4), hands the file's name to libpq as bytes in the system's ANSI code page (up to 6.3.5 as Latin-1 bytes, which on code page 1252 are the code page's own for U+00A0 to U+00FF), and libpq looks for the file by those bytes and then hands the same bytes to OpenSSL, whose file opening on Windows reads a name as UTF-8 first and opens the file at that reading when one is there. When every byte of the name outside ASCII also reads as UTF-8 - for example U+00C3 U+00A9, the bytes C3 A9 on code page 1252, which are U+00E9 in UTF-8 - the database server's certificate was checked against the file at that other name whenever one was there, which allows a local attacker who can create that file but cannot change the configured one, as any user can by default beside a file an administrator keeps under ProgramData, or beside a folder directly under the system drive's root whose permissions the administrator restricted, and who can intercept the connection to the database server or stand in for it, to have hMailServer trust a certificate authority of the attacker's own and read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database, the database password included; the file alone, holding no authority that issued the database server's certificate, stops hMailServer from connecting to its database. The same applies in 6.3.4 through 6.3.7 to TlsCaFile when an Oracle MySQL client library has been put in place of the bundled MariaDB Connector/C, since that client opens the file through OpenSSL in the same way; the bundled MariaDB Connector/C opens the file in the code page and is not affected, and neither are the Linux builds. The configuration is not the default: by default no root certificate file is named.

advisories.summary: The web services listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.3 through 6.3.7 does not apply the...
advisories.description: The web services listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.3 through 6.3.7 does not apply the server's IP ranges to the connections it accepts, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing account passwords at the listener's sign-ins after the auto-ban has banned the attacker's address. The listener is off by default (WebServicesHttpPort and WebServicesHttpsPort 0). From 6.3.3 its CardDAV, and from 6.3.4 its CalDAV and its Outlook Autodiscover answer to a request that carries credentials, sign an account in with HTTP Basic over HTTPS. A failed sign-in there counts towards the auto-ban as a failed logon on any other protocol does: when the failures counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 within 30 minutes by default), the server writes an IP range that refuses the address for AutoBanMinutes (60 by default), and the SMTP, POP3, IMAP and ManageSieve listeners refuse it. The web services listener asked no IP range when it accepted a connection (in 6.3.3 nothing, from 6.3.4 the country policy alone), so it went on serving such an address, whether its ban had been earned there or on another protocol, and also an address that an administrator's IP range allowing nothing holds. Each failed sign-in there closed only its own connection, and the next connection was accepted, during the ban and after it. The firewall rule and command the auto-ban can drive (AutoBanFirewall and AutoBanCommand, off by default) are told only the SMTP, POP3 and IMAP ports, so that the firewall rule and the packaged hook did not close the listener's ports, and the fail2ban jail packaged for Linux (off by default) lists only the mail and ManageSieve ports. The only limit left on the guesses at one account there was the per-name lockout (AccountLockoutThreshold in hMailServer.ini, 0, off, by default), which has a separate defect fixed in the same release. The flaw is reached on the listener's HTTPS port: behind a TLS-terminating proxy the listener sees the proxy's address for every client, and a ban never named the client there.

advisories.summary: The ARforms plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the ...
advisories.description: The ARforms plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'description' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 7.2.4 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The injected payload is deserialized via maybe_unserialize() when an administrator views the affected entry; if the attacker's array contains a 'referrer' key, the attacker-controlled page_url and http_referrer values are used as-is and rendered unescaped into the admin entry detail view.

advisories.summary: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.3 through 6.3.7 on Windows, with a MySQL or MariaDB database,...
advisories.description: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.3 through 6.3.7 on Windows, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, hands the bundled MariaDB Connector/C the folder of its authentication plugins (the plugin folder in the installation's Bin folder) as Latin-1 bytes, which the client reads in the system's ANSI code page when it builds a plugin's path and loads the plugin with LoadLibraryExA, which allows a local authenticated user to execute code as the hMailServer service's account (LocalSystem, or the service's virtual account for a new installation from 6.3.4) by creating the folder those bytes name in the code page and placing in it a DLL with a plugin's name, when the installation folder's path holds a character between U+0080 and U+00FF whose byte the code page reads as another character, and none above U+00FF, and the user can create that other folder (by default any authenticated user may create a folder directly under the root of the system drive). The server converted the path with the C runtime's wcstombs_s in the C locale, which writes each character up to U+00FF as the byte of the same value: on code page 1252 those bytes are the same letters, while on another code page, such as 1251, or on a UTF-8 code page, they name another folder. The client loads the plugin the database server names in its greeting, unless it is built in, and any plugin the server names in an authentication switch, and tries again at each connection while a load fails, so with a MySQL 8.0 or later server, whose greeting names caching_sha2_password by default, the DLL is loaded at the next connection the service makes, whatever plugin the database account uses; a DLL's entry point runs when it is loaded. A path holding any character above U+00FF was handed over as an empty string, whatever the code page, from which the client makes a plugin's name at the root of the current drive: for the service, whose current folder is System32, that is the root of the system drive, where by default only administrators can create a file, but the server's own database commands (hMailServer.exe --check-database, --upgrade-database and the others from 6.3.4, and the /Debug and /Test console modes from 6.2.3) run in the folder they are started from - the product tells administrators to run them from an elevated prompt in the Bin folder, and the setup of 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 ran two or three of them itself with the Bin folder as their working folder for a new installation with an external database - so a DLL that a local authenticated user placed under a plugin's name at the root of a drive other users may write, such as a FAT or exFAT volume, was loaded into the administrator's process at the command's first connection to a MySQL 8.0 or later server. 6.3.8 fixes both cases: it hands the folder in the code page's bytes or by its short (8.3) name, and where neither can be written, a folder under the Windows system folder that holds no plugin and that only administrators can create, or else refuses the connection before attempting it; it never hands the empty value or a folder the current drive completes. The configuration is not the default: the default installation folder, under Program Files, is ASCII. Linux builds set no plugin folder and are not affected.

advisories.summary: Allocation of resources without limits in the JSON reader of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.2...
advisories.description: Allocation of resources without limits in the JSON reader of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.2 through 6.3.7 allows a remote attacker to exhaust the server's memory and hold its threads, making mail delivery, the REST API and the webmail unavailable. The reader built a tree of values far larger than the text it read, copying each value into every level above it, and set no bound on the number of values, so a single JSON document of many small values, within the 16 MB the server reads, raised the service's memory by about 2 GB and held one thread for seconds to minutes. From 6.3.4 a remote unauthenticated attacker reaches the reader by mailing such a document as a TLS-RPT report, up to 16 MB once decompressed, to a hosted domain's report mailbox, where an administrator has set one; it is read on a mail delivery thread (ten by default), and those threads deliver all mail, local and outbound. From 6.3.4 it is also reached without an account through the reply to a password-protected message, with the message's link alone, where the REST API is on (it is off by default) and a public base URL for such links is set; and by any account, from 6.3.2 through the webmail's send and draft routes and from 6.3.4 through its other routes granted 16 MB and the send API; the webmail's send, draft and settings routes parsed the body again for each member read. The REST API serves every request on four worker threads, in the process that also serves SMTP, IMAP and POP3, so a few such documents at once make it unavailable and can exhaust the machine's memory and end the whole service. This is a separate defect from CVE-2026-107574, the reader's handling of duplicate member names, fixed in 6.3.6.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

advisories.summary: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 through 6.3.7, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, TlsMode...
advisories.description: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 through 6.3.7, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, TlsMode=verify-full and no TlsCaFile, does not verify the database server's certificate's issuer or name when the connection is one that MariaDB Connector/C treats as local - Server= set to 127.0.0.1, ::1 or localhost (on Linux a Unix socket), to . on Windows (a named pipe), or to a comma-separated list of servers that holds such an element - which allows a local attacker who can stand in for the database server, for example by listening on its port while it is stopped or restarting, to receive the database sign-in, the password included, and to read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database. hMailServer applied verify-full by turning the client's certificate verification on without a CA file, but MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.1 and later, on a connection they treat as local and with no CA file, accept any certificate within its validity period that is self-signed or sent with its own root, for any name (Connector/C 3.4.2 to 3.4.10 also one whose issuer they cannot find), so the client accepted the certificate an impostor made, asked no proof of the password and allowed a switch to an authentication method that sends the password unhashed, while hmailserver --check-database said the certificate had been checked against the system's trust store and the application log that it had been checked. The Windows builds bundle Connector/C 3.4.9 (6.3.4 to 6.3.6) and 3.4.11 (6.3.7); on Linux the distribution's client is used, and Connector/C 3.3 and 3.4.0 and Oracle's MySQL client are not affected. The configuration is not the default: TlsMode defaults to prefer, which checks no certificate.

advisories.summary: The ARForms plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file upload in all versions up to,...
advisories.description: The ARForms plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file upload in all versions up to, and including, 7.2.4 via its form file-upload handler. The name of the stored file is taken from an attacker-controlled request header and is not adequately restricted to safe file types, and the plugin's file-type and content-safety checks can be evaded, allowing files that contain executable PHP code to be written to a publicly accessible directory. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to upload malicious files to the affected site's server, which may make remote code execution possible. Exploitation requires a published form containing a File field to be publicly accessible on the site.

advisories.summary: Improper link resolution in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through...
advisories.description: Improper link resolution in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.7 allows a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's service account or as an administrator when the path to the program folder passes through a junction, a symbolic link or a mount point that the user controls or that every user may change, such as a junction made at the root of a drive, which takes the root's permissions, or through a folder that every user may rename. Setup installed the programs through any such link without first checking who controls it, or whether a folder above the program folder may be renamed, and the service is registered to run the programs by that path, so the programs are installed where a link another account controls leads, or that account can later make the path lead to a folder it controls; the service, which runs as LocalSystem or as its virtual account, and the programs administrators run from Bin are then started from there. 6.3.7's fix for CVE-2026-107571 does not cover this: its hardening of the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel does not change a folder reached through a link that the administrators do not alone control, and setup does not refuse such a path: it installs through the link and at most reports afterwards that the folders could not be hardened. The default installation under Program Files is not affected.

A delegated administrator can exploit this to move a group they control under an administrative group, causing all members to inherit full realm-admin privileges and gain complete control over the realm.

advisories.description: A flaw was found in gnutls. This vulnerability occurs because permitted name constraints were incorrectly ignored when previous Certificate Authorities (CAs) only had excluded name constraints. A remote attacker could exploit this to bypass critical name constraint checks during certificate validation. This bypass could lead to the acceptance of invalid certificates, potentially enabling spoofing or man-in-the-middle attacks against affected systems.

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in sequoia-openpgp. The library incorrectly infers key flags for older...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in sequoia-openpgp. The library incorrectly infers key flags for older certificates when a key flags subpacket is missing, leading to a discrepancy in how key capabilities are viewed. This key flag confusion allows an attacker to bypass the back-signature check. Consequently, an attacker can illegitimately bind an arbitrary subkey to their own certificate and forge signatures, completely compromising cryptographic integrity.

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in sg3_utils. The sg_inq command, when invoked with the --export option, outputs...

A newline character embedded in a device-supplied name string can inject arbitrary properties into the udev device database. This could allow an attacker who can present a crafted SCSI device to execute arbitrary commands as root when the device is disconnected.

advisories.summary: The Security For WooCommerce WordPress plugin through 1.0.16 does not restrict access to several...
advisories.description: The Security For WooCommerce WordPress plugin through 1.0.16 does not restrict access to several of its REST API routes, allowing unauthenticated users to generate login tokens for every user and then retrieve them, and so log in as any user, including administrators.

advisories.summary: The Event Tickets and Registration WordPress plugin before 5.30.3.1 does not restrict attendee...
advisories.description: The Event Tickets and Registration WordPress plugin before 5.30.3.1 does not restrict attendee data to events the requester is allowed to view, allowing unauthenticated users to retrieve the attendees of private and other non-public events.

advisories.summary: The AskAny  WordPress plugin before 2.2.0 does not validate the extension or content of files...

advisories.summary: The Limit Login Attempts Security  WordPress plugin before 3.4.2 does not validate the...
